note: What the text of the OpenAPI specification defines that none of its published schemas holds. A list made by hand, and a floor. Every statement is in this repository's own words; no text of the specification is reproduced. Section numbers are those of 3.2.1, but for a row true of 3.1 only, whose numbers are those of 3.1.2.

constructs.says: The major and minor parts of `openapi` select the feature set; the patch part is ignored.
A deprecated field keeps its whole meaning and is read like any other.
The text gives some constructs the status "undefined" or "implementation-defined"; a model needs a way to say a construct has that status.
Field names and map keys are case-sensitive unless the text says otherwise.
The bodies an API description describes need not be JSON or YAML.
A name or value that maps to an HTTP concept follows the case rules of HTTP: header names, an authentication scheme, the token of a runtime expression.
A `description` is CommonMark, at version 0.27 or later.
A relative link inside CommonMark resolves where the text is rendered, not against the base of the document.
`$self` is the identity of the document and its base URI; a reference to the document targets it.
Absent or empty `servers` means one server whose `url` is `/`.
A list of security requirements is a choice of one; the schemes inside one requirement all apply; an empty requirement makes security optional.
The order of `tags` carries meaning; a tag an operation names need not be declared.
A webhook describes a request the provider of the API makes, the reverse of a path; its key is a name unique among webhooks.
A description may be several documents, one of which is the entry document; only the entry document's paths add URLs to the API.
A reference may target a document by `$self`, or a schema by `$id`, `$anchor` or `$dynamicAnchor`; it is unresolvable only after every document given has been parsed.

There are two kinds of address: a URI that identifies part of the description, resolved against the base of the document, and a URL of the API, resolved against the server. Any field that holds a URI may hold a relative one.
The base URI comes from four sources in the order RFC 3986 gives; a relative `$self` is resolved first. A schema under an `$id` is referenced through the nearest `$id`.
A relative reference in a schema uses the nearest parent `$id` as its base; elsewhere the base is that of the referring document.
The fragment of a reference into a JSON or YAML document is a JSON Pointer (RFC 6901).

Four connections are made by name and not by reference: a security requirement's key to a security scheme, a discriminator's value to a schema, an operation's tag to a tag, and a link's `operationId` to an operation. The text recommends resolving component and tag names from the entry document.
How a name is resolved from a document that is not the entry document is left to the implementation.
What kind of object a value is comes from where it is reached, so one value reached two ways may be read as two kinds.
References may form a cycle.
A server `url` is a template: a variable is substituted where it is named in braces. 3.2 gives the grammar in ABNF.
A URL of the API resolves against the server URL; in 3.2 `$self` plays no part in it.
The `default` of a server variable is the value substituted and sent when no other is given, unlike the `default` of a schema.
The `enum` of a server variable limits the values that may be substituted.
A component has no effect on the API unless something outside the components refers to it.
The full URL is the server URL, resolved and substituted, with the path appended and not resolved against it.
A path with no template is matched before one with a template; an ambiguous match is for the tool to settle.
An empty Paths Object, and an empty path item, mean something: the reader may not be permitted to see what is there.
Each template expression of a path is bound by name to a path parameter, of the path item or of each of its operations.
The value of a path parameter holds no unescaped `/`, `?` or `#`. 3.2.1 adds that a template variable never matches a value holding a forward slash.
A path template has a grammar, given in ABNF.
Each template expression corresponds to a path parameter; in 3.2 each appears at most once in a path.
Each server variable appears at most once in a server URL, and its `default` is one of its `enum`.
What a path item with `$ref` means where a field is given both beside the reference and in its target.
The `summary` and `description` of a path item apply to every operation under it.
A parameter is identified by its name and its location together. A parameter of a path item applies to every operation under it; an operation may override it by that identity and cannot remove it.
`servers` on an operation replaces that on its path item, which replaces that of the document.
The key of `additionalOperations` is the HTTP method exactly as it is sent, with its capitals. `query` is the QUERY method (RFC 10008 in 3.2.1).
`operationId` is the identity of an operation, and is case-sensitive.
An absent `deprecated` means false, on an operation, a parameter and a header.
A request body is allowed on any method; what it means on a method for which HTTP defines no content is not well defined.
`security` on an operation replaces that of the document; an empty list removes it.
A parameter in `querystring` is the whole query string as one value, described by `content`; its `name` is not used.
A `querystring` parameter appears at most once and never with a `query` parameter.
Parameter names are case-sensitive; header names are not.
A header parameter named `Accept`, `Content-Type` or `Authorization` is ignored.
What a header parameter named `Cookie` means.
The `name` of a parameter is not part of what is serialised for `querystring`, nor for some combinations of `style` and `explode`.
An absent `required` means false; for a path parameter it must be present and true.
`allowEmptyValue` says an empty value stands for a parameter that is not used. Absent means false. It applies to `query` only, and is ignored where the style cannot serialise the value.
A parameter is serialised in one of two ways: by `schema` and a style, or by `content` and a media type. 3.2.1 says the same rules govern reading a value back.
The value of a header parameter or a cookie parameter is passed through with no percent-encoding.
An absent `style` means `form` in `query` and `cookie`, and `simple` in `path` and `header`.
An absent `explode` means true for the `form` style, and in 3.2 the `cookie` style, and false for every other.
`explode` has no effect on a primitive value, nor in 3.2 on `deepObject`.
What `explode: false` means with the `deepObject` style.
In 3.2.1, `explode: false` is not valid for a parameter in `cookie`.
`allowReserved` selects the reserved expansion of RFC 6570; absent means false. In 3.2 it applies wherever the location or style percent-encodes; in 3.1 to `query` only.
An `example` or `examples` of a parameter, a header or a media type overrides the `example` of its schema.
Each style is a function from a value, a primitive, an array or an object, to text, defined by RFC 6570 or by the specification.
A combination of style, explode and type outside the table is not permitted; a cell the table marks "n/a" is undefined.
The `cookie` style follows the Cookie syntax of RFC 6265, with no escaping.
How the `deepObject` style writes a property that is itself an array or an object.
Percent-encoding follows RFC 3986 for a URL; a form body follows the WHATWG URL standard in 3.2 and RFC 1866 in 3.1, with `+` for a space. A character used as a delimiter is never encoded.
What a serialised value includes: the name for the `form` style, the leading delimiter for `matrix` and `label`, and never the `?`, the `&` or a header's name.
In the table of styles an undefined value is that of RFC 6570: an empty string is not undefined.
A key of `content` is a media type or a range of them; where several match, only the most specific applies.
An absent `required` on a request body means false.
The `schema` of a media type describes the whole content.
A media type that is a sequence of values is read as an array in the same order; `itemSchema` describes each value.
Server-sent events are described as the parsed event; a field given no type is a string.
`encoding` applies by property name, to multipart and form bodies. Each item of an array property becomes one part under the same name.
A key of `encoding` that matches no property is ignored. 3.2.1 says how a body is read back: repeated names gather into an array in order.
A key of `encoding` must be a property of the schema, and `encoding` applies to request bodies only.
`prefixEncoding` and `itemEncoding` apply by position, as `prefixItems` and `items` do, to a multipart body.
On binary content that is not encoded as text, a length counts octets.
A media type with no `schema` describes content that is unconstrained or binary; a `format` does not set an encoding.
An absent `contentType` of an encoding is taken from the type of the property and its `contentEncoding`, by a table. For an array it is `application/json` in 3.2 and that of the items in 3.1.
In 3.2.1 the `contentType` of an encoding has a grammar in ABNF: media ranges of RFC 9110, separated by commas.
A `Content-Type` among the `headers` of an encoding is ignored; `headers` is ignored outside multipart.
Giving any of `style`, `explode` or `allowReserved` on an encoding selects serialising by style, and `contentType` is then ignored. It applies to form bodies only.
In `multipart/form-data` nothing is percent-encoded and `allowReserved` has no effect.
An encoding may hold encodings: one level must be supported.
A form body is percent-encoded after its complex values have been written as text.
`contentEncoding` on a part of a multipart body stands for a `Content-Transfer-Encoding` header; `contentMediaType` gives way to `contentType`.
The `default` response stands for every status code the Responses Object does not give.
A response for an exact status code takes precedence over one for its range.
A key of the Responses Object is a status code, or a range written as a digit and `XX`.
A response header named `Content-Type` is ignored; the names of response headers are case-insensitive.
A key of a callback is a runtime expression, or a URL holding expressions in braces, evaluated against the request and response that trigger it. The expression has a grammar in ABNF.

An example is given as data (`dataValue`) or as it is serialised (`serializedValue`, `externalValue`). `value` and the short `example` mean the serialised form, and stand for the data where the two are the same in JSON.
The characters of an `externalValue` are read as UTF-8 where nothing says otherwise.
A link targets an operation by `operationRef`, a URI reference, or by `operationId`, a name.
A key of a link's `parameters` is a parameter name, which a location and a dot may precede. A value is a constant or a runtime expression.
A runtime expression that fails gives no value to the target operation.
A runtime expression keeps the type of the value it refers to; its `name` is case-sensitive and its `token` is not.
A link's `operationId` names an operation that exists and is unique; an `operationRef` points to an operation.
A header is a parameter whose name is its key in the map and whose location is the header.
For a header, an absent `required` means false, an absent `style` means `simple`, the only style allowed, and an absent `explode` means false.
A header value is not percent-encoded and is not quoted for the author: it arrives already quoted and escaped.
For `Set-Cookie`, each value is on a line of its own, without the name.
The `application/linkset` media type is described by a schema written for its JSON form.
Whether `allowReserved` may be given on a header: 3.1.2 forbids it; 3.2 no longer says so and lists no such field.
A tag's name is the identity an operation's `tags` refer to. In 3.2 `parent` names the tag it is nested under and `kind` is a category.
A tag's `parent` names a tag that exists, and the nesting has no cycle.

The `summary` and `description` of a Reference Object replace those of its target, and do nothing where the target has no such field. Any other field beside the reference is ignored, unlike beside a `$ref` in a schema.
The dialect of a schema is settled in order: `$schema` at the root of a schema resource, then `jsonSchemaDialect`, then the dialect of the version. 3.2.1 names that dialect by a dated address.
A schema may hold a keyword of any vocabulary, or any property at all; the `x-` prefix is not needed inside a schema.
A `format` a tool does not recognise is treated as though it were absent.
An integer is a mathematical one: 1 and 1.0 are the same value and both are integers.

Data has three forms: as serialised, as data, and as the application holds it. For content that is not JSON, the type of a property is found by following only `$ref` and `allOf`; a schema that gives no type allows every type.
`contentMediaType` gives way to the key of the media type or to `contentType` where they disagree.
`readOnly` and `writeOnly` are annotations of direction; whether a value sent against them is an error is for the owner of the API.
Composing schemas with `allOf` makes no hierarchy between them.
A `oneOf` or `anyOf` whose every member is a `const` with annotations may be read as an enumeration with a description for each value.
A discriminator is a hint and never changes whether a value validates.

With no mapping, the discriminating value is the name of a schema component. A mapped value is a name or a URI reference: where it could be either it is a name, and a leading `./` makes it a reference. A schema written in line is not a candidate.
A discriminator on a parent schema makes every schema that builds on the parent by `allOf` an alternative: the relation is read from the children.
`defaultMapping` names the schema for a value that is absent or has no mapping.
What a discriminator means when the discriminating property is absent.
`defaultMapping` is required where the discriminating property is optional.
How a key of `mapping`, a string, is matched to a value that is not a string; and any arrangement of `oneOf`, `anyOf`, `allOf` and a discriminator the text does not describe.
An absent `nodeType` means none where the schema holds `$ref`, `$dynamicRef` or the array type, and an element otherwise; absent `attribute` and `wrapped` mean false.
An absent XML `name` is taken from the name of the component or of the property.
The order of nodes written from an object.
An element of a primitive type has a text node that is not written down.
A null is written as an element marked `xsi:nil`, and as an attribute left out.
An XML namespace is an IRI in 3.2 and a URI in 3.1, and is not relative.
The `scheme` of an HTTP security scheme is case-insensitive.
A key of a security requirement is the name of a security scheme component or a URI; where it could be either it is a name, and a leading `./` makes it a URI.
The values of a security requirement are scopes for OAuth2 and OpenID Connect, and names of roles for every other kind.
A key of a security requirement names a security scheme that is declared.
The value of an `x-` field may be any JSON value. Names beginning `x-oai-` and `x-oas-` are reserved. A Reference Object takes no extension.
A key of a map of components, and the name of a link, matches a pattern of letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`.
How a typed value that is not a string is written as text.
Each style corresponds to an operator of RFC 6570; several form parameters make one list of variables; a name RFC 6570 does not allow is percent-encoded first.
How an unencoded `+` is read back depends on whether the form rules or the URI rules apply; a delimiter inside a value must be encoded.
